text: With a trained defect-detection model in hand, Solari Vision Labs now needs to actually serve it -- and manufacturing customers only send real traffic in short bursts around each shift change, with hours of nothing in between. This lab builds a serving endpoint that genuinely scales to zero when idle, and scales on real GPU utilization when it's busy, instead of paying for an always-warm GPU replica.

The Deployment itself looks like Chapter 4's inference architecture: GPU node selector, a readiness probe with a sixty-second initial delay for model loading, and a resource limit of one GPU. It starts at one replica, but that number is temporary -- once the autoscaler is wired in, this Deployment stops controlling its own replica count entirely.

That autoscaler is a single KEDA ScaledObject with two triggers doing two different jobs. A queue-depth trigger answers whether any replica should exist at all, taking the Deployment from zero replicas to one the moment a request actually arrives. A GPU-utilization trigger then answers a separate question -- once that one warm replica is actually saturated past seventy percent, it scales further, all the way up to eight.

A cooldownPeriod of five minutes keeps a short lull between uploads from forcing a fresh cold start on the very next one. But scale-to-zero creates a real conflict with Chapter 4's PodDisruptionBudget pattern: a minAvailable of one can't be guaranteed on an endpoint that's deliberately allowed to run zero replicas. Solari's platform team makes that tradeoff on purpose, skipping the PDB here and accepting the small risk of a drain during a genuinely idle window.

Proving it works means watching three distinct states against real traffic: zero replicas while idle, exactly one replica once the first request's cold start clears, and more than one replica once a simulated shift-change burst actually pushes GPU utilization past the threshold. Each half of the scaler gets verified separately, not assumed from the YAML.

Solari now has a GPU training cluster and a serving endpoint that only spends money while it's actually working. Lesson 31 turns to the opposite failure mode -- a training run that kept burning GPU spend for days after it had already finished, because nobody was watching for it.
